Introduces Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view, cited in abbreviated form.

ranges.en: Cites R' Yochanan: a wound worth less than a perutah brings lashes, and striking is not compared to cursing. Then quotes the resident-alien clause.

Rebbi Yochanan answers: those fit for recitation from the recitation, and those not fit from when they see the Temple courtyard
Objects that the answers conflict, since recitation and placing are each contradicted
No contradiction: one view is Rebbi Shimon's and the other the Sages, and the placing view is Rebbi Yehuda's
Asks what the view of the Sages is against Rebbi Yehuda
A baraita of Rebbi Yehuda: the verse says and you shall place it, meaning waving, while another verse says place it, meaning placing
Explains that the verse means waving, and the other verse is the placing
Asks who is the Tanna who disagrees with Rebbi Yehuda
It is Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, as taught in a baraita
Cites the verse that the priest takes the basket from your hand, teaching that first fruits require waving, per Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view as attributed
Asks what the reason of Rebbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is
Derives it from the repeated words hand and priest and owner in verses on offerings, showing the offering is waved in the same manner
Asks how this works in practice
The priest places his hands under the owner's hands and waves
Rava bar Adda reports Rebbi Yitzchak on first fruits

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from when first fruits become liable, once they see the face of the Temple, and whose view this is
A baraita of Rebbi Eliezer: partly outside and partly inside, the outside ones are like unconsecrated food and the inside ones like consecrated
Rav Sheshet holds that for first fruits, placing is essential but recitation is not essential
Identifies this view with the Tanna of a baraita
A baraita of Rebbi Yosi: three things from three elders; Rebbi Yishmael proposes that one might bring second tithe to Jerusalem now and eat it there
Argues by a kal vachomer from the firstborn, which needs bringing to a place, that second tithe also needs bringing and is limited to the Temple
Cites the verse on eating before God and derives that second tithe is equated with the firstborn, also needing a place
The verse equates second tithe to the firstborn, so second tithe is also only before the Temple
Objects: if so, first fruits are more stringent since they need recitation and placing, so the analogy should be refuted
Rav Ashi replies that the stranger's first fruits are a case where the law should be re-examined before it is refuted
The argument is refuted in one respect, since the two have a common side with the altar
Asks what the view is on holiness: whether the earlier holiness sanctified for a time and for the future, also for the firstborn
Asks the same about the other view, whether the firstborn also needs to be examined
Ravina answers that the view holds holiness applies for a time only, and here the firstborn was sprinkled before the Temple was destroyed while its flesh remained
Compares the flesh to the blood: as the blood is on the altar, so the flesh is on the altar
Objects that an analogy is taught by analogy again, since second tithe of grain is ordinary food

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what can be said for the one who follows the teacher, if the law follows the learned teaching
Blood and flesh are one matter, so the same reasoning applies to both
We learned in a mishna that second tithe and unredeemed sacred items are treated as holy food for those who eat them
Rebbi Yosi bar Chanina: the later clause on second tithe is clean when the eater is clean and eats outside the wall; the earlier clause is unclean and he eats in Jerusalem
Asks from where one is liable for eating second tithe in a state of impurity
A baraita of Rebbi Shimon cites the verse I have not removed from it while impure, and distinguishes impure-pure cases
Asks where one is warned about eating in impurity
Rebbi Shimon replies that the impurity of the body is explicit in the verse about the holy things
Cites the verse on a person who touches an impure thing and may not eat the holy things
Asks from where the impurity of the person himself is derived
Derives from the verse you may not eat in your gates, and the later verse saying the impure and the pure may eat it in your gates
A baraita of the school of Rebbi Yishmael: impure and pure may eat from one dish without concern
The Torah asks how an impure thing permitted to you is with a pure thing there, while here you may not eat it
Asks from where Rebbi Elazar derives that redemption applies to impure second tithe
Derives from the verse you cannot carry it that carrying means eating, citing the verse in Genesis where Joseph carried food from before him
Rebbi Biby and Rebbi Asi derive that second tithe that is clean may be redeemed even one step outside the wall
Cites the verse for you cannot carry it as the source
Objects that this verse is needed for Rebbi Eliezer, and if so the verse should say you cannot eat it, and carrying the whole would have been stated differently
Concludes that we learn two things from the verse
Rebbi Chanina and Rebbi Hoshaya ask about the case of the gate of Jerusalem
Obviously, if one is outside and carries inside, the case is clear
Asks about the reverse case, where the walls take hold of him inside and he carries outside
An elder in the school of Rebbi Shimon bar Yochai taught them the answer
Cites the verse that the place is far from you, supporting the elder's teaching
Rav Pappa holds a piece of reed and asks, and it is left unresolved
Rebbi Asi reports Rebbi Yochanan: one becomes liable for second tithe once one sees the face of the wall
Asks what the reason is for that ruling
Cites the verse that you shall eat it before God in the year after year
Explains the verses by the places where each phrase applies, so that in each case the prohibition follows the eating
Objects from a baraita of Rebbi Yosi on a priest who had a fig of untithed produce, with the various tithes and their places

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the case: one who eats a forbidden fig is lashed once if it was in Jerusalem, and three times if outside the wall
Objects that even if he does not see the wall, they go in and out, so what is the point of the case
Asks what case we are dealing with here
Explains: the case is where they brought the gifts in as tevel, and the view is that untithed gifts count as tithed
Objects from a baraita of Rebbi Yosi that the Houses of Shammai and Hillel did not dispute produce whose work was complete
The houses dispute produce whose work was complete and passed through Jerusalem: Shammai says return the second tithe and eat in Jerusalem, Hillel says redeem and eat anywhere
Objects that if untithed gifts count as tithed, the walls would take hold of him
Rabbah: a wall for eating is Torah law, a wall for taking hold is rabbinic, and the rabbis did not decree when the item is in its tevel state; Ravina gives a case of holding by a reed
Mishna: one who makes a bald spot on his head, or cuts the corners of his beard, or cuts a cut for the dead, is liable
One who cuts one cut for five dead, or five cuts for one dead, is liable for each one
The mishna details the cuts on the head and the beard, two on each side and one below
Rebbi Eliezer holds that if all are removed at once he is liable only once, and liable only if he removes them with a razor
Rebbi Eliezer adds that even if he plucked them with tweezers or a blade he is liable
A baraita cites the verse that they shall not make a bald spot, and derives that each bald spot is a separate liability
Asks why the verse says on their heads
Cites the verse on not making a cut between your eyes for the dead
One might think liability applies only to the space between the eyes
Asks from where the whole head is included
The verse on their heads includes the whole head
The rule applies only to priests, where the verse adds extra commandments, and not to Israelites in general
Asks from where the same applies to Israelites
Derives the Israelite rule from the common word baldness in the other verse, by a verbal analogy
Applies the same analogy: liable for each bald spot, and for the head just as between the eyes
Just as there the prohibition is for the dead, so here it is also for the dead
Asks how these four or five bald spots are to be understood: one after another with five warnings, or otherwise

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether one who is liable with one warning incurs liability at all
Objects from a mishna on a nazirite who drinks wine all day: liable once, but if warned each time, liable for each
Explains that the mishna is needed for one who anointed his five fingers, so the warnings were separate for each
Asks what is the measure of a bald spot
Rav Huna says enough to be seen from the head; Rebbi Yochanan reports a view of the size of a grain; others say enough to be seen
Rav Yehuda bar Chabiba reports three tannaim: one says a grain, one says enough to be seen, one says two hairs, with a rule for a case of removing and reinserting
A baraita: one who removes a mouthful of a pair in a week is liable
Asks what measure a mouthful of a pair is
Rav Yehuda says two
Objects that a baraita says the same for a bald spot, two, so the same measure is taught
The baraita repeats that one who removes a mouthful of a pair is liable, and the measure is two
Rebbi Eliezer says one, and the Sages agree with Rebbi Eliezer on plucking white hairs from among black ones, where even one is liable
Cites the verse that a man shall not wear a woman's garment, showing the prohibition applies even in sand
Mishna: one who surrounds the corners of his head
A baraita defines the end of the head: the line from the temples to behind the ear and to the forehead
A Tanna taught before Rav Chisda that both the surrounder and the one surrounded are lashed
Rav Chisda objects, mocking the claim with the case of one who eats dates in a basket
Whose view is it? Rebbi Yehuda's, who holds a negative without action incurs lashes
Rava says the case is one who surrounds for himself, and all agree on that
Rav Ashi says the case is one who assists, and all agree on that
Mishna: one who mars the corner of his beard
A baraita defines the end of the beard as the locks of the beard
Mishna: one who makes a single cut
A baraita cites the verse on making a cut for the dead, and the word for soul limits liability to the dead
So one is liable only for the dead
Asks from where one is liable for five cuts on one dead
The verse says and he shall cut, to make one liable for each cut
Rebbi Yosi says one cut for five dead is also a case of liability for each
Asks from where this is derived
The verse for a soul is used to make one liable for each soul
Objects that the house that fell and the ship that sank were already excluded from the verse

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rebbi Yosi holds that cutting and gashing are one matter, and Shmuel rules that one who cuts with a tool is liable
Objects from a baraita that cutting is by hand and gashing by a tool, which would be the view of Rebbi Yosi
A Tanna taught before Rebbi Yochanan: for the dead, cutting by hand or tool is liable; for idolatry, by hand liable, by tool exempt
Objects that the verse reads the reverse, with swords and spears, so the rule should be stated the other way
Mishna continues: liable for a cut on the head
Rav Sheshet marks the place as between the joints of the head
Mishna: two cuts on each side of the beard and one below
Rav Sheshet marks the place as between the joints of the beard
Rebbi Eliezer holds that if one removes them, he is liable only if he removes them with a razor, as one case
A baraita cites the verses on not shaving the corners of the beard and not destroying it, and derives that the shaving must involve a razor
Rebbi Eliezer says that even plucking with tweezers or a blade makes one liable
Asks whether the gezerah shavah requires a razor, or whether scissors also count
Rather, one always learns the gezerah shavah, and holds that these also count as shaving
Mishna: one who writes a tattoo but does not prick, or pricks but does not write, is not liable
Liable only when one both writes and pricks by hand, with blue or any material that marks
Rebbi Shimon ben Yehuda, in Rebbi Shimon's name, holds one is liable only if he writes the Name
Cites the verse on not putting a tattoo on yourselves, I am the Lord
Rav Acha son of Rava asks Rav Ashi whether this means he must write I am the Lord literally
Rav Ashi replies that as Bar Kappara taught, one is liable only if he writes the name of idolatry, as the verse says I am the Lord and not another
Rav Malkiya reports Rav Adda bar Ahava: it is forbidden to put ash of a burnt coal on a wound because it looks like a tattoo
Rav Nachman son of Rav Ika lists remedies Rav Malkiyo and others permitted or forbade
Asks what the difference is between the mishna and the baraita as the sages report them
There is a difference in the case of a wound; Rav Ashi says wherever there is a wound, the wound testifies on it
Mishna: a nazirite who drinks wine all day is liable once, but liable for each warning when warned each time
Mishna: a nazirite who defiles himself for the dead all day is liable once, but for each warning if warned each time
Mishna: a nazirite who shaves all day is liable once, but for each warning if warned each time
Mishna: a nazirite who wears mixed fabric all day is liable once, but for each warning if warned each time

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one who plows a furrow is liable for eight prohibitions, including plowing with ox and donkey together and sacred and mixed things
Rebbi Chananya ben Chachinai adds that one who wears mixed fabric is liable, and they answer that it is not the name, and he replies the nazirite is not either
Rav Biby reports Rebbi Yosi that undressing and dressing count as one act, and Rav Ashi holds one is liable even without pausing beyond the time to undress and dress
Repeats the mishna about one who plows a furrow
Rebbi Yannai says a group concluded that one who covers with mixed kinds is lashed, and Rebbi Yochanan says this is our mishna
Quotes the mishna of the furrow with the eight prohibitions as Rebbi Yochanan reads it
Asks how the plowing case can be liable for mixed kinds, when the plowing of the ox is covered as it goes
Rebbi Yochanan's rebuttal by example: if the plow pulled a stone, a pearl could not be found underneath
Resh Lakish says that if not for a flattering remark, he would say this mishna is Rebbi Akiva's, who holds that one who maintains mixed kinds is lashed
Asks what Rebbi Akiva's view is, and what is taught in a baraita
Taught in a baraita: one who weeds or covers mixed kinds is lashed
Rebbi Akiva adds that one who maintains mixed kinds is also liable
Asks what the reason is for Rebbi Akiva's view
Cites the verse on not sowing your field with mixed kinds, and derives from the verse on not crossbreeding that maintaining is also liable
Ulla objects to Rav Nachman: then one should also be lashed for sowing on a festival
Rav Nachman responds that the Tanna did not teach this, and the Tanna's list includes only eight
Rava holds that there is a distinction among labors on Shabbat, but none on a festival
Abaye objects to Rava: but we learned there is no distinction among labors on a festival, citing the mishna on cooking a sinew in fat
Mishna: one who cooks a sinew in fat on a festival and eats it is liable five times, for each prohibition violated

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if the liability were for kindling, one would not be liable; he is already liable for cooking, and a baraita of Rebbi Chiya says two for eating and three for cooking
Derives the case where one removes kindling and brings in Asherah wood, with the warning from the verse about not cleaving to what is banned
Rav Acha son of Rava asks Rav Ashi whether one should also be lashed for the verse about not bringing an abomination into the house
Explains the case as cooking in sacred wood, with the warning from the verses on burning the sacred objects and not doing so to God
Gloss gives a mnemonic for the list of verses
Rav Hoshaya objects: one should also count sowing in an ever-flowing valley, which has its own warning
Rav Chananya objects: one should also count erasing the Name on the way, with its warning from the verse about destroying their name
Rebbi Avahu objects: one should also count cutting off a bright spot, with the warning from the verse about the plague of leprosy
Abaye objects: one should also count removing the breastplate from the ephod and the rings of the ark, with its warning
Rav Ashi objects: one should also count plowing in Asherah wood, with the warning from the verse about not cleaving to what is banned
Ravina objects: one should also count cutting down good trees, with its warning from the verse about not cutting them
Rebbi Zeira objects to Rebbi Mani: count one who vowed not to plow on a festival, since the oath does not take effect there and he is bound since Sinai
Rebbi Mani replies: for example one who vowed not to plow on weekdays or festivals, since the oath takes effect on weekdays, it takes effect on festivals as well
Notes that the case of an item borrowed is not taught in the baraita
Objects with the counterexamples of sanctity in the firstborn and the nazirite's status of Samson, who was a nazirite for defilement only for the dead
Rather this Tanna does not hold that a general prohibition covers each case separately
Rebbi Hoshaya holds one who mates an ox with unfit consecrated animals is lashed twice
Rebbi Yitzchak holds one who leads an ox with unfit consecrated animals is lashed, since it is one body that the verse treats as two bodies
Mishna: how many lashes are given, forty less one
Cites the verse on lashing with a count of forty as the source for the forty
Asks from where we know that the number is near forty
Rebbi Yehuda holds forty full lashes are given
Asks where the extra lash is given, between the shoulders
One measures the person only with lashes that can be divided, and they measured him to receive forty
The lashes are given forty, and he is lashed partially

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if they estimated he could take forty, and after lashing he proved unable, he is exempt; if estimated for eighteen and then can take forty, he is exempt
Asks why the verse is needed if the forty are counted in number
If the verse says forty in number, it means the count sums up to forty
Rava jests that people stand before a Torah scroll and not before a great man, because the scroll says forty and the Sages came and cut it to one less
Rebbi Yehuda holds forty full lashes are given, distributed between the shoulders
Rav Yitzchak asks what the reason of Rebbi Yehuda is
Cites the verse on the blows between your hands, from the house of my beloved
The Rabbis hold that verse is about the children of Rabban's house
One estimates only for lashes that can be divided
Asks whether he was lashed or not, and raises a contradiction
Objects from a baraita: if he was estimated to take forty and then reconsidered and was found unable, he is exempt, and vice versa
Rav Sheshet: not a difficulty, one case is estimated for one day and the other for the next day, and the other day after
Mishna: one who transgresses an offense with two prohibitions, if one estimate covers it, lashed and exempt; otherwise lashed, healed, and lashed again
Objects from a baraita: one estimate may not be applied to two prohibitions
Rav Sheshet: not a difficulty, one case was estimated for forty-one and the other for forty-two
Mishna: how they lash him: his two hands tied to the pillar, the attendant holds his garments, the strap of a calf folded, two straps of a donkey, one-third in front and two-thirds behind
Cites the verse: the judge shall cast him down, and the striker strikes with one hand with all his strength
The reader recites the verses of curse and blessing, and returns to the beginning of the reading
If he dies under the lashes, the striker is exempt
If he added one strap and he died, the striker is exiled for it; if he was injured, whether in the sun or in water, the striker is exempt
Rebbi Yehuda holds that the man is lashed in the sun and the woman in water

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the reason is, since the offender is disgraced
Rav Sheshet reports Rebbi Elazar ben Azarya's question of where the strap is taken from a calf
Cites the verse forty he may strike, placed next to the verse not muzzling the ox while threshing
Derives from the same verse that a levirate wife who fell before a man with a skin disease may not be muzzled, citing the verse on brothers dwelling together
Rav Sheshet reports Rebbi Elazar ben Azarya: one who despises the festivals is like one who worships idols
Cites the verse on not making molten gods, placed beside the verse on keeping the festival of matzot
Derives from the verse on casting to the dogs that one who spreads slander, accepts slander, or testifies falsely deserves to be cast to dogs
Mishna: the strap of a donkey
Derives from the verse on the ox knowing its owner and the donkey its master, the length of the donkey's strap
The hand's width is a handbreadth
Abaye infers that each strap is used according to its need
Rava objects: if so, there would be many straps
Rava rather says the strap has a cord, which is pulled tight when needed and loosened when not
Mishna: they lash him
Rav Kahana derives from the verse that the judge shall cast him down and strike before him according to his wickedness, and only one strike for the one wickedness
Mishna: they do not lash him beyond
Rebbi Yochanan derives from the verse on casting down that the strap is doubled
The striker strikes with his hand
The Sages hold attendants are placed only if they are weak in strength and strong in knowledge; Rebbi Yehuda holds even weak in knowledge and strong in strength
Rava says it is reasonable to follow Rebbi Yehuda
Cites the verse that he shall not add lest he add
Argues: if the attendants are weak in knowledge, the warning is needed, but if they are strong in knowledge, why would they need warning
The Sages hold that one only urges one who is ready, and the Sages hold the attendant only encourages
The striker raises his hands both ways and strikes with one hand, so that the strike is not from his own hand
The reader reads
The chief judge reads, the second counts, and the third says to strike, lengthening if the strokes are many and shortening if few
Objects that we learned: he returns to the beginning of the reading, which is a mitzvah to be exact, and if not exact, he returns to the start
A baraita: the verse on not adding teaches that the first strokes are the great strokes, so that few strokes are not added to
Mishna: if the strap broke and he was lashed
A baraita: whether man or woman, in the sun and not in water, is Rebbi Meir's view; Rebbi Yehuda holds the man in the sun and the woman in water; the Sages hold either case
Objects from Rebbi Yehuda's view that man and woman alike are in the sun
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that both are equal in the sun
Shmuel holds that if they bound him and he ran away from the court, he is exempt
Objects from a baraita that if the strap broke in the second or the first, the strap breaking in the second is exempt, and asks why the case differs
A baraita: if they estimated he would be lashed and he was slightly lashed, exempt if he leaves the court; if slight, lashed; and even if slight at first, lashed
Mishna: all who are liable for karet who were lashed are free from their karet
Cites the verse: your brother shall be lightly beaten before your eyes, so that when lashed, he is like your brother, per Rebbi Chananya ben Gamliel

Rebbi Chananya ben Gamliel argues a fortiori from one who transgresses and takes his soul, to one who does a mitzvah and is given his soul; Rebbi Shimon derives it from the verse on those who are cut off

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the verse that a man shall live by doing the statutes, as the basis for the principle
One who sits and does not transgress receives a reward like one who does a mitzvah

Rebbi Shimon bar Rebbi derives by a fortiori from the verse on blood being the life: if one who abstains from blood gets reward, one who abstains from theft and forbidden unions gets more for his descendants
Rebbi Chananya ben Akashya holds that God wished to grant merit to Israel, so He gave them much Torah and commandments, citing the verse
Rebbi Yochanan reports that his colleagues disputed with Rebbi Chananya ben Gamliel
Rav Adda bar Ahava reports that between Shabbat and Yom Kippur the difference is that one's intent is with men and the other's with karet, and that it is all with men
Rav Nachman says this is Rebbi Yitzchak's view, that karet-liable are not lashed, as taught
Rebbi Yitzchak's baraita: karet-liable are included among the lashed, and the sister case is singled out for karet
Rav Ashi says even if one says the Rabbis, the principal intent is with men in one case and with Heaven in the other
Rav Adda bar Ahava reports Rav: the law follows Rebbi Chananya ben Gamliel
Rav Yosef asks who went up and came back, to report the matter in the heavenly court
Abaye objects with a teaching of Rebbi Yehoshua ben Levi: three things the lower court did, and the heavenly court agreed with them
Asks again who went up and came back
Rather we interpret verses, and so too we interpret verses here
Rebbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: three things the lower court did, and the heavenly court agreed with them
Cites the verse on reading the Megillah, which says the Jews kept what they had accepted below, and the heavenly court agreed
Cites the verse on greeting, where Boaz greets the reapers with the Lord be with you
Cites the verse in Judges saying the Lord is with you, mighty man of valor
Objects that one might say Boaz acted on his own, so the proof does not hold
Cites the verse in Malachi on bringing all the tithe into the storehouse as the third matter
Continues the verse: I will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing, until there is no more need
Asks what until there is no more sufficiency means
Ramei bar Rav: until your lips are tired of saying enough
Rebbi Elazar says the Holy Spirit appeared in three courts: the court of Shem, the court of Shmuel, and the court of Solomon
Derives from Judah's case in the court of Shem, with a bat kol saying more righteous than I
Derives from the court of Shmuel, citing the verse where he says whose ox have I taken, and they answer that he was not defrauded
Derives from the court of Solomon, citing the verse that the king said give her the living child, since she is his mother
Asks how Solomon knew, perhaps she was being clever
A bat kol came out and said she is his mother
Rava objects: from where do we know that Judah was not counting months and days and the other was not clear
All Israel are called by the singular form, as in Israel is saved in the Lord, and Solomon's case likewise, not a verse but a Gemara

Rebbi Shimlai teaches that six hundred and thirteen commandments were said to Moses: three hundred and sixty-five prohibitions, matching the days of the sun, and two hundred and forty-eight positives, matching the limbs of a person
Rav Hamnuna cites the verse that Moses commanded us the Torah, which has the numerical value of six hundred and thirteen

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The six hundred and thirteen commandments were heard from the mouth of the Almighty, with a mnemonic for the first commandments
David came and reduced them to eleven, as the verse in Psalms says
Cites Psalm fifteen on who may dwell in God's tent and walk in integrity, speak truth, and not slander
Applies the verse: the one who walks in integrity is Abraham, and the one who works righteousness is Abba Chilkiyah
Applies the verse: one who speaks truth in his heart is Rav Safra, and the one who does not slip with his tongue is Jacob
Cites the verse from Genesis where Jacob says perhaps my father will feel me
Applies the verse: one who does no evil to his fellow and bears no reproach against his kin, the one who brings near his relatives
Hezekiah, who dragged his father's bones on a rope bed, is the one who honors those who fear the Lord
Jehoshaphat, who when he saw a Torah scholar stood from his throne, embraced and kissed him, and called him my father, my master
One who swears to do harm and does not change, as Rebbi Yochanan
Rebbi Yochanan, who fasted until he returned home, did not give his money at interest
Even at interest to a gentile, and does not take a bribe against the innocent, as Rebbi Yishmael son of Rebbi Yosi
Rabban Gamliel wept whenever he reached this verse, saying who does all these things
Asks who does all these things, and whether one who keeps all will never fall, while one who breaks one may
They reply: the verse says does these, not all these, so even one of them suffices
Cites the verse on not defiling yourselves by all these, and argues that the parallel verse likewise means one of them
Concludes the same holds here: one of all these
Isaiah came and reduced them to six, as the verse says
Cites Isaiah's verse: he who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, despises gain of oppression, shakes off bribes, stops his ears, and shuts his eyes from evil
The one who walks righteously is Abraham our father
Cites the verse from Genesis: for I know him, that he will command
The one who speaks uprightly is one who does not shame his fellow in public, and despises gain of oppression, as Rebbi Yishmael ben Elisha
Examples: one who shakes off bribes, one who stops his ears from hearing blood, one who shuts his eyes from seeing evil, including the case of a man not looking at women at the washing
Cites the verse: he shall dwell on high
Micah came and reduced them to three, as the verse says
Cites the verse: it has been told to you, man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you, to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God
Explains the three: doing justice is the law, loving mercy is acts of kindness, walking humbly is accompanying the dead and bringing in a bride
Argues a fortiori: if humbly, which is not usually done in private, the Torah says walk humbly, then things usually done in private certainly
Isaiah returned and reduced them to two, as the verse says
Cites the verse: keep justice and do righteousness
Amos came and reduced them to one, as the verse says: seek Me and live
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: say seek Me in all the Torah, rather than only one
Habakkuk came and reduced them to one, as the verse says: the righteous shall live by his faith
Rebbi Yosi bar Chanina: Moses decreed four decrees on Israel, and four prophets came and annulled them
Moses said: Israel shall dwell in safety alone, the eye of Jacob
Amos came and annulled it, as the verse says: stop, I ask, who can stand, Jacob
The verse says the Lord relented concerning this
Moses said: and among those nations you shall find no rest
Jeremiah came and said: go to give rest to Israel
Moses said: visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children
Ezekiel came and annulled it, as the verse says: the soul that sins shall die
Moses said: you shall perish among the nations
Isaiah came and said: on that day a great shofar shall be blown
Rav said: I am afraid of this verse, you shall perish among the nations
Rav Pappa objects: perhaps it is like the lost sheep, as the verse says I have gone astray like a lost sheep, seek your servant
Rather it is from the end of the verse, your enemies' land shall eat you
Mar Zutra objects: perhaps it is like eating cucumbers and gourds; and the anecdote of Rabban Gamliel, Rebbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rebbi Yehoshua and Rebbi Akiva walking on the road

Anecdote: they heard the cry of Rome from a distance of a hundred and twenty miles and began to weep, but Rebbi Akiva laughed, and explained that the Romans bow to idols while Israel is oppressed in its own land

ranges.en: The people say the fire has burned it and we will not weep
Rebbi Akiva answers that this is why he laughs: if those who transgress his will are so treated, those who fulfill it will be rewarded even more
Story: once they went up to Jerusalem, tore their garments at the Mount of Olives, and at the Temple Mount saw a fox come out of the Holy of Holies and began to weep

Rebbi Akiva laughed; they asked why, and he asked why they wept; they said the place where a non-priest who approaches shall die is now walked upon by foxes, so they will not weep; he replied that this is why he laughs
Cites the verses of Isaiah and Micah on Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah, showing that Zechariah's prophecy is tied to Uriah's, and Zechariah's verse of elders in the streets
Rebbi Akiva says: I feared that Zechariah's prophecy would not be fulfilled, and now that Uriah's is fulfilled, Zechariah's is surely fulfilled in this manner
It is known that Zechariah's prophecy is fulfilled in this manner
His students said: Akiva, you have comforted us, Akiva, you have comforted us
Closing formula: the chapter of those who are lashed, and the tractate of Makkot is concluded
